This noise is freq. used as a simile for sweet sounds, , , , , , etc.; and Plato calls them οἱ Μουσῶν προφῆται, ; but they also became a prov. for garrulity, λαλεῖν τέττιξ: τ. πολλοὶ γινόμενοι νοσῶδες τὸ ἔτος σημαίνουσι. They were thought to sing continually without food or drink, , ; or on a diet of air and dew, , , (), , . The Greeks ate τέττιγες to whet the appetite, , cf. , , (anap.), (anap., unless here the τέττιξ ἐνάλιος is meant, v. infr. ); and as a medical remedy, , .
